svg.text: Drop in a sample → it stains, images, counts and classifies microplastics with YOLOv8 on a Raspberry Pi → shows SAFE / NOT SAFE and logs the result. No phone needed.
Concept sketch · v0.1 · based on FLOro [1]
No phone · no chemicals to handle

g.text: 1 drop on the membrane → push in
blue working · green safe · red not
The limit (particles per litre) is a setting. WHO (2019) found no health-based
guideline value for microplastics in drinking water [4], so none is hard-coded.
Cartridge QR ID · time · location · count · polymer mix · raw image
→ saved on microSD (CSV + images), synced over Wi-Fi when in range
Staining and imaging happen in one sealed chamber: the unit pulls the cartridge in, dispenses Nile Red,
dries it with the fan and waits in the dark, then images under 395 nm UV through the yellow filter.
The Pi runs YOLOv8 on the image and shows the result. The user never touches the dye or a microscope.
395 nm UV LED pair, built in
NR in acetone, 15 min dark, by hand [1]
Phone-based YOLO detection reached 98 % accuracy with a $10 lens [3], which supports a low-cost camera path.
Nile Red limits: organic matter can also stain (false positives), and black/rubber particles can be missed [1][2].
MPx values in the right column are design targets, not measured results.
[1] Rermborirak et al. (2025). Low-cost portable microplastic detection system integrating Nile Red fluorescence staining with YOLOv8-based deep learning (FLOro). J. Hazard. Mater. Adv. 19, 100787.
[2] Leonard et al. (2022). Smartphone-enabled rapid quantification of microplastics. J. Hazard. Mater. Lett. 3, 100052.
[3] Arju et al. (2025). Deep-learning enabled rapid and low-cost detection of microplastics in consumer products. RSC Adv. 15, 10473.
[4] World Health Organization (2019). Microplastics in drinking-water. ISBN 978-92-4-151619-8.
